args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a driving licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: This case directly quotes the Supreme Court in Lehru: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.' This is the governing standard for what an owner must do.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes the low threshold for owner verification: a facial check of the licence suffices. The owner need not conduct a background investigation with the RTO.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Even where a conscious and wilful breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence) is established, the insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to the third party and may only recover the amount from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured, and the onus is on the insurer to prove it.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court held that even when the driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence while driving a goods vehicle (commercial), the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This confirms that the insurer's defence of 'breach' does not defeat the claim against the insurer — it only entitles recovery.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that proving breach does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party; it only gives recovery rights. The insurer's defence is not a complete shield.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: The Full Bench held that under Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if a fundamental breach of policy conditions is proved, and can recover from the insured. The only exception is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively settles the law: even fundamental breach does not defeat the third-party claim against the insurer. The insurer must pay and then recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority that failing to check the licence (even if it amounts to a fundamental breach) does NOT defeat the insurer's liability to the third party. The insurer's only remedy is pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach... and the insurer proves the said breach in view of the mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court examined the owner's duty in the context of a driver lacking a badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle. The insurer proved the breach but was still directed to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that even where the insurer successfully proves the driver was not duly licensed (missing badge/endorsement), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
supporting.quote: The insurer and insured are bound by the conditions enumerated in the Policy and the insurer is not liable to the insured if there is violation of Policy conditions... [but] the doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer is directed to pay compensation first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no licence at all. The owner failed to produce the driver's licence. The tribunal held this was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — driver with no licence at all — results in pay-and-recover, not absolution of the insurer. This is the strongest supporting precedent for the proposition that failing to check does not defeat the insurer's defence.
supporting.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability... [but] the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver does not hold a valid licence during the interregnum. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, accident on 02-07-2008, renewal on 04-07-2008. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a lapsed licence (where the owner arguably failed to check currency) results in pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a special endorsement required for driving a goods carriage carrying hazardous goods, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid licence for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but lacked the special endorsement for a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The court held this was a breach but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the pay-and-recover principle to cases involving special endorsements required under the CMV Rules, showing the breadth of the principle.
supporting.quote: Once it was established that there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer is jointly and severally liable with the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even an expired licence (which the owner failed to check) does not let the insurer off the hook. They will say the insurer is jointly liable without even a pay-and-recover order.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2001 Tribunal decision that predates the settled line of Supreme Court authority (Swaran Singh, Lehru, etc.) which consistently grants pay-and-recover. The Full Bench in Yallavwa (doc_025) now governs: the insurer must pay and recover, but the pay-and-recover order is the standard remedy, not joint liability without recovery. Also, this case involved licences that were renewed shortly after the accident, showing the drivers were not disqualified — a weaker breach than a completely absent or fake licence.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid liability to third parties merely because the driver of an LMV lacked an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable without a pay-and-recover order.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that where the driver holds a valid licence for the class of vehicle (LMV), the mere absence of a commercial endorsement is not a breach at all — the insurer is directly liable with no right of recovery.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific finding that a Mahindra Maxi Cab is an LMV and the driver held an LMV licence. The Supreme Court held there was no breach at all because the licence covered the vehicle class. This is distinguishable where the driver had no licence at all, a fake licence, or a licence for a completely different class of vehicle. Where the breach is genuine (no licence, expired licence, wrong class), the pay-and-recover principle applies.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh principles (pay-and-recover) apply only to third-party claims, not to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will not cite this — it actually helps the insurer on the own-damage point. However, the insurer must be careful: this case limits Swaran Singh to third-party claims. If the matter involves an own-damage claim (e.g., the owner suing the insurer for vehicle damage), the insurer CAN defeat the claim by proving a fake licence. This is adverse to the insurer's position in own-damage cases.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly limits its holding to own-damage/non-third-party claims. For third-party claims (which is the typical motor accident claim), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle continue to apply. The insurer should concede this case applies only to own-damage scenarios.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach. The insurer is absolved of direct liability but must pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite the pay-and-recover part (they get their money). But the insurer can use the finding of 'fundamental breach' to argue that the owner was at fault and must indemnify the insurer. The risk is that the tribunal might not grant a pay-and-recover order if the insurer fails to prove the breach properly.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position that a fundamental breach exists and the owner is liable to indemnify. The only risk is evidentiary — the insurer must properly prove the breach. The case itself confirms the pay-and-recover remedy.

priority_arguments: 1. The owner's duty to check a driver's licence is limited to a facial examination: if the licence looks genuine on its face and the driver appears competent, the owner has discharged their duty (doc_027, citing Lehru). The owner is NOT required to verify with the RTO.

2. Even if the owner failed to check the licence (or the licence is invalid/expired/fake), the insurer's statutory liability to the third party under Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act remains intact. The insurer must pay the third party and can only recover from the insured (doc_025 — Full Bench; doc_033; doc_035; doc_024).
3. The only exception to pay-and-recover is where the third party played fraud or was in collusion with the insured (doc_025). This is a very narrow exception.
4. For own-damage claims only, the insurer can defeat the claim entirely by proving a fake/invalid licence (doc_031 — Laxmi Narain Dhut). This does NOT apply to third-party claims.

5. The burden of proving breach is on the insurer. The insurer must show not just that the licence was invalid, but that the owner was conscious of or wilfully permitted the breach (doc_033, citing Swaran Singh and Lehru).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: 1. If the insurer fails to lead adequate evidence of the licence defect (e.g., fails to examine the RTO or produce the licence verification report), the tribunal may hold the insurer directly liable without any recovery rights.

2. If the driver held a valid licence for the class of vehicle but lacked only a commercial endorsement/badge, the Supreme Court in S.Iyyapan (doc_032) may be cited to argue there was no breach at all — the insurer is liable without recovery.

3. In own-damage claims, the insurer CAN defeat the claim entirely by proving a fake licence (doc_031). Counsel must identify whether the matter is a third-party claim or an own-damage claim at the outset.
4. If the licence was expired but renewed within 30 days, Section 15 of the MV Act deems it continuously valid — the insurer may have no defence at all.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal: admit statutory liability to the third party, but aggressively seek a pay-and-recover order against the insured owner. Lead evidence of the licence defect through the RTO/MVI. In own-damage claims (consumer forum or civil court): argue that Swaran Singh does not apply and seek complete absolution from liability under Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031).

caveats: This corpus does not contain the text of the Supreme Court's decisions in Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 or Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which are the foundational authorities on this subject. They are cited extensively in the corpus judgments and their principles are embedded in the ratio of doc_027, doc_033, doc_025, and others. Counsel should read the full text of Swaran Singh and Lehru directly.

The corpus contains no judgment where the insurer was completely absolved of third-party liability due to the owner's failure to check the driver's licence. Every case in this corpus that found a licence defect ordered pay-and-recover. This is consistent with the settled legal position.
doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is the only insurer-favouring judgment on licence issues, and it is expressly limited to own-damage claims.

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

In the instant case, the tractor in question (No. U.P. 35-B 1649) was duly insured with the insurance
company. Admittedly, no separate premium was paid for the trolley. This was the specific defense

ctor means a motor vehicle which is not itself constructed to

On a perusal of the definition of word 'tractor' shows that the tractor itself is not able to carry any
load without the equipments. Therefore, any equipments attached to the tractor is a part of the
tractor and covered under the insurance policy.
In view of the above, we observed that the trailer/trolley, which is attached with the tractor is a part
of the tractor, which was duly insured from the insurance company. Hence, the insurance company
cannot escape from its liability to pay compensation by taking the plea that the trailer was not
separately insured.
But in the instant case, fact remains that at the time of accident, the trolley which was attached with
the tractor was carrying the Iron Rods and Bricks for the purpose of construction of a room to cover
the pakki boring as admitted by the appellant in paragraph-3 of the affidavit. Transportation of iron
rods and bricks is certainly not an agricultural activity. The tractor was insured only for the purpose
of agricultural activity. The tractor will have to be used only for agricultural purpose not for any
other purpose including the construction of a room. Thus, there is a violation of the terms and
conditions of the insurance policy. When it is so, then we are of the view that in the instant case, the
insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation and the owner of the tractor will have to

In view of the aforesaid, the appeal is dismissed.

(Delivered by Hon'ble Dr. Satish Chandra, J) This appeal is filed under Section 173 of the Motor
Vehicles Act, 1988 against the judgment and order dated 27.01.2009 passed by Motor Accident
Claims Tribunal, Unnao in Claim Petition No. 117 of 2001 whereby an award of Rs.1,18,850/- was
awarded against the appellant.
The brief facts of the case in narrow compass are that on 02.12.2000, one Sri Arvind Kumar was
going on scooter to see off his relative. When he reached near Hyderabad Paisara, one Tractor No.
U.P. 35-B 1649 took a sharp turn. The Iron Rods loaded in the trolley (trailer) attached to the tractor
in question hits the deceased Arvind Kumar, who died on the spot. The FIR was lodged. The Tractor
was insured but trolley was not insured. So, the liability was fixed against the owner of the Tractor
i.e. appellant by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal for Rs.1,18,850/-. Being aggrieved, he filed the
present appeal.
During the course of argument, learned counsel for the appellant submits that the trailer is the part
of the tractor and tractor was duly insured. Independently, the tractor or trolley is not of any use.
With the tractor, some equipments or trolley will have to be attached for the purpose of agricultural
activity. He further submits that trailer/trolley falls within the definition of the vehicles, as such, it is
an attachment made to the prime mover of tractor and it has no independent driving system.
Therefore, it is not required to be insured under the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and
insurance company is liable to pay the compensation.
According to the appellant's counsel, deceased was driving the scooter without holding any valid
license.

trailer was defined as motor vehicle, which was intended to drawn by a motor vehicle. Thus, it is
evident that it is not a mechanically propelled vehicle either power of propulsion is transmitted from
external or internal sources. Therefore, even though, Section 2 (46) embraces trailer within the

definition of 'motor vehicle' or 'vehicle', but further distinction has to be drawn between the vehicle
and motor vehicle and that distinction has to be carved out on the basis of the specific definition
given to the word trailer. Therefore, while all the motor vehicles may fall within the definition of
vehicles, but, all the vehicles are not motor vehicles. The trailer as such is an attachment made to the
prime mover either a tractor or a mechanical contrivance and it has no independent propulsion. The
trailer always is a detachable container, which does not have any independent driving system. Its
movements are dependent on the prime mover, such as tractor, motor vehicle etc. Hence, insurance
of trailer is not a mandatory requirement under the provisions of Section 146 of Motor Vehicles Act
and if the prime mover/motor vehicle/tractor is insured and the negligence of the driver of the said
motor vehicle is established, the compensation is payable by the owner of the tractor and insurer
irrespective of the fact whether the victim suffers injury with the tractor or with the trailer.
Therefore, we are of the view that in such cases, the insurance company is also liable along with the
owner of the tractor/trailer to pay compensation.

payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal Ratlam / Madhya Pradesh High Court
payload.holding: The High Court held that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle, dismissed the owners' appeal regarding negligence and quantum, and dismissed the claimants' cross-objections for enhancement.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger travelling in a goods vehicle is a gratuitous passenger whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 95 of the Motor Vehicles Act and is not covered by the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer cannot be held liable for compensation.

payload.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
payload.court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Bombay Bench At Aurangabad
payload.holding: The Tribunal erred in passing an order of 'pay and recover' against the insurance company when passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not third parties and their risk is not covered under the Act policy, and therefore the insurer is completely exonerated.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal or Court cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award and recover from the owner.

Company Ltd. Vs. Asha Rani [AIR 2003 SC 607]. It has been laid down that the term "any person"

Whether the learned Member, Motor Accident Claims Tribunal was justified in passing order of 'pay

REASONS 7 It has been vehemently submitted on behalf of the appellant that the defence, that was

Policy". The said policy does not cover the risk of the occupants. As per Section 147 of Motor
Vehicles Act, question that is required to be answered is, whether the risk of said occupant is
covered under the terms of policy. Tribunal had considered only Section 147(2) of the M.V.

o.1 towards passengers and
therefore, the Tribunal had come to a conclusion that there was breach of policy under Section
149(2)(A)(ia) of the Motor Vehicles Act. In fact, before the Tribunal also many Judgments of Apex
Court were referred, however, based on the 9 FA_2021_2018_Jd decision in Saju P. Paul (supra)
the learned Tribunal had passed the order of pay and recover.
11 Now those various pronouncements relied by both sides are required to be considered. In Baljit
Kaur's case, it was the case, wherein person travelling in goods vehicle as gratuitous passenger was
involved. Taking into consideration the earlier pronouncements it was observed -
"Therefore, instead and in place of the insurer the owner of the vehicle shall be liable
to satisfy the decree. However, since the law was not clear so long, the legal position
as clarified herein shall have prospective effect. Therefore, in the interest of justice
will be subserved if the appellant herein (insurance company) is directed to satisfy
the awarded amount in favour of the claimant, if not already satisfied, and recover
the same from the owner of the vehicle."

Thereafter, this ratio was followed in many other cases. In Manuara Khatun's case (supra) taking
note of Saju P. Paul's case it was observed -
"We find no merit in any of the submissions. Firstly, as mentioned above, we find
marked similarity in the facts of this case and the one involved in Saju P. Paul case.
Secondly, merely because the compensation has not yet been paid to the claimants
though the case is quite old (16 years) like the one in Sanju P. Paul case, it cannot be a
ground to deny the claimants the relief claimed in these appeals. Thirdly, this Court
has already considered and rejected the argument 10 FA_2021_2018_Jd regarding
not granting of the relief of the nature claimed herein due to pendency of the
reference to a larger Bench as would be clear from para 26 of the judgment in Saju P.
Paul. That apart, the learned counsel for the appellants stated at the Bar that the
reference made to the larger Bench has since been disposed of by keeping the issue
undecided.

Constitution of India to pay the compensation amount and later on recover it from the owner of the
vehicle." However, the reference that was made has been disposed of on 17-09- 2013 by keeping the

14 FA_2021_2018_Jd needs to be set aside.

from opponent No. 01.

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a driving licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: This case directly quotes the Supreme Court in Lehru: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.' This is the governing standard for what an owner must do.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes the low threshold for owner verification: a facial check of the licence suffices. The owner need not conduct a background investigation with the RTO.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Even where a conscious and wilful breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence) is established, the insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to the third party and may only recover the amount from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured, and the onus is on the insurer to prove it.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court held that even when the driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence while driving a goods vehicle (commercial), the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This confirms that the insurer's defence of 'breach' does not defeat the claim against the insurer — it only entitles recovery.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that proving breach does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party; it only gives recovery rights. The insurer's defence is not a complete shield.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: The Full Bench held that under Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if a fundamental breach of policy conditions is proved, and can recover from the insured. The only exception is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively settles the law: even fundamental breach does not defeat the third-party claim against the insurer. The insurer must pay and then recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority that failing to check the licence (even if it amounts to a fundamental breach) does NOT defeat the insurer's liability to the third party. The insurer's only remedy is pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach... and the insurer proves the said breach in view of the mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court examined the owner's duty in the context of a driver lacking a badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle. The insurer proved the breach but was still directed to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that even where the insurer successfully proves the driver was not duly licensed (missing badge/endorsement), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
supporting.quote: The insurer and insured are bound by the conditions enumerated in the Policy and the insurer is not liable to the insured if there is violation of Policy conditions... [but] the doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer is directed to pay compensation first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no licence at all. The owner failed to produce the driver's licence. The tribunal held this was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — driver with no licence at all — results in pay-and-recover, not absolution of the insurer. This is the strongest supporting precedent for the proposition that failing to check does not defeat the insurer's defence.
supporting.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability... [but] the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver does not hold a valid licence during the interregnum. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, accident on 02-07-2008, renewal on 04-07-2008. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a lapsed licence (where the owner arguably failed to check currency) results in pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a special endorsement required for driving a goods carriage carrying hazardous goods, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid licence for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but lacked the special endorsement for a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The court held this was a breach but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the pay-and-recover principle to cases involving special endorsements required under the CMV Rules, showing the breadth of the principle.
supporting.quote: Once it was established that there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the tanker had no valid licence. The Tribunal directed pay-and-recover. The High Court upheld this, confirming the principle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority: no valid licence → pay-and-recover, not absolution.
supporting.quote: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer is jointly and severally liable with the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that even an expired licence (which the owner failed to check) does not let the insurer off the hook. They will say the insurer is jointly liable without even a pay-and-recover order.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2001 Tribunal decision that predates the settled line of Supreme Court authority (Swaran Singh, Lehru, etc.) which consistently grants pay-and-recover. The Full Bench in Yallavwa (doc_025) now governs: the insurer must pay and recover, but the pay-and-recover order is the standard remedy, not joint liability without recovery. Also, this case involved licences that were renewed shortly after the accident, showing the drivers were not disqualified — a weaker breach than a completely absent or fake licence.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid liability to third parties merely because the driver of an LMV lacked an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable without a pay-and-recover order.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that where the driver holds a valid licence for the class of vehicle (LMV), the mere absence of a commercial endorsement is not a breach at all — the insurer is directly liable with no right of recovery.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific finding that a Mahindra Maxi Cab is an LMV and the driver held an LMV licence. The Supreme Court held there was no breach at all because the licence covered the vehicle class. This is distinguishable where the driver had no licence at all, a fake licence, or a licence for a completely different class of vehicle. result.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a driving licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: This case directly quotes the Supreme Court in Lehru: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.' This is the governing standard for what an owner must do.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes the low threshold for owner verification: a facial check of the licence suffices. The owner need not conduct a background investigation with the RTO.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Even where a conscious and wilful breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence) is established, the insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to the third party and may only recover the amount from the insured. The breach must be on the part of the insured, and the onus is on the insurer to prove it.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court held that even when the driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence while driving a goods vehicle (commercial), the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This confirms that the insurer's defence of 'breach' does not defeat the claim against the insurer — it only entitles recovery.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that proving breach does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party; it only gives recovery rights. The insurer's defence is not a complete shield.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: The Full Bench held that under Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if a fundamental breach of policy conditions is proved, and can recover from the insured. The only exception is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively settles the law: even fundamental breach does not defeat the third-party claim against the insurer. The insurer must pay and then recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority that failing to check the licence (even if it amounts to a fundamental breach) does NOT defeat the insurer's liability to the third party. The insurer's only remedy is pay-and-recover.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court examined the owner's duty in the context of a driver lacking a badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle. The insurer proved the breach but was still directed to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that even where the insurer successfully proves the driver was not duly licensed (missing badge/endorsement), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer is directed to pay compensation first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no licence at all. The owner failed to produce the driver's licence. The tribunal held this was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even the most extreme case — driver with no licence at all — results in pay-and-recover, not absolution of the insurer. This is the strongest supporting precedent for the proposition that failing to check does not defeat the insurer's defence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has expired and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver does not hold a valid licence during the interregnum. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, accident on 02-07-2008, renewal on 04-07-2008. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a lapsed licence (where the owner arguably failed to check currency) results in pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a special endorsement required for driving a goods carriage carrying hazardous goods, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid licence for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but lacked the special endorsement for a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The court held this was a breach but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the pay-and-recover principle to cases involving special endorsements required under the CMV Rules, showing the breadth of the principle.
supporting.quote: Once it was established that there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the tanker had no valid licence. The Tribunal directed pay-and-recover. The High Court upheld this, confirming the principle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority: no valid licence → pay-and-recover, not absolution.
